newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Army clashes with rebels in volatile south Albania.
newsitem.headline: Army clashes with rebels in volatile south Albania.

text.p: Albania's army clashed with rebels in volatile southern regions in its drive to extinguish resistance to President Sali Berisha.
Opposition groups, generally demoralised by the imposition of emergency rule last weekend, issued an appeal to the West on Wednesday to persuade Berisha to accept a political settlement.
Western countries mounted a campaign to end the violence which has killed at least 20 people in the past week.
But Albanian authorities portrayed life as normal throughout the impoverished Balkan country.
A delegation from the Council of Europe, which oversees human rights, arrived for talks and a European Union mission headed by the Dutch foreign minister was due later in the week.
Eyewitnesses saw the army withdraw in trucks after 40 minutes of fighting with armed groups east of the port of Sarande, near the Greek border.
They saw at least four fighters and two soldiers hurt and hospital officials said one man was in a serious condition.
"The people won. The army, about 60 soldiers, got in their trucks and drove away," Sarande's former prefect Dimitris Stefos told Reuters in Athens by telephone.

One wounded insurgent told reporters the army had operated under the shoot-on-sight order which went into effect on Monday, the same day parliament re-elected Berisha to a second term. The assembly, where Berisha's Democratic Party holds nearly all the seats, had introduced the state of emergency the previous day.
Sarande residents, contacted from Athens, said rebels staged an evening rally in a main square, defying a curfew, and holding guns and babies aloft while chanting anti-government slogans.
Army tanks and armoured personnel carriers roamed roads near the main regional town of Gjirokaster, 30 km (18 miles) north of the border, a Reuters correspondent in the area reported.

The Health Ministry in Tirana said two people had died from gunfire in the port of Vlore further north -- site of some of the fiercest clashes sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment funds with the life savings of hundreds of thousands.
Anger over the failed pyramid schemes has spread across the country and at the weekend rioters burned and looted in the border region. They stole thousands of arms from state arsenals.
The capital remained quiet, though armed police patrolled squares and intersections. Berisha suggested cutting the overnight curfew by three hours in Tirana and other unaffected towns.
State television showed shops and services operating normally throughout the country of 3.2 million and reported measures by local "defence councils" to fight price gouging.
"It was hard to distinguish today from any normal day," a reporter said of the town of Kavaje, west of Tirana. "Food and water supplies are normal, but prices rose two to five percent."
Television also showed what it said was an arsenal of 4,500 weapons handed in by residents of Fier, another southern flashpoint of recent disturbances.
